system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one so that a reader
cannot tell what field, subfield, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, but can still see the research
trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

For each item return:
- "abstract_problem": the decision problem as a generic research trade-off (one or two sentences, at most 40 words).
- "abstract_choice": what was chosen, over what alternative when one is given, and the stated reason if any (one or
  two sentences, at most 45 words). Start it with "Chose to".

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, benchmarks, methods,
  organisations, people, papers, phenomena and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area (for example
  AI, machine learning, language models, neural networks, training, fine-tuning, prompts, attacks, security,
  privacy, policy, labs, governments, biology).
- Use only generic research vocabulary: system, method, intervention, treatment, condition, measurement, signal,
  effect, baseline, control, sample, variant, procedure, dataset, outcome, claim, hypothesis, collaborator, audience.
- Keep the structure of the trade-off (for example speed vs rigour, breadth vs depth, a bold vs a hedged claim,
  a direct vs an indirect measurement, a natural vs a constructed setting, continue vs stop) and the direction chosen.
- Add nothing that is not in the source: no judgement, praise or new detail. Never say who made the decision.
- Write every item in the same plain style and at a similar length.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "abstract_problem": ..., "abstract_choice": ...}, ...]} with one entry per input
item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:d4cee8f27af2",
  "problem": "How to let interpretability tools be tested without the predictor trivially recovering the ground-truth counterfactual outcome.",
  "did": "They restricted predictor agents to read-only access to the target model's internals, excluding steering and activation patching, and measured uplift over a transcript-only baseline.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "allowing interventions such as steering",
   "activation patching",
   "editing the prompt"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The label is itself the outcome of an input intervention, so an intervening predictor could approximate the ground-truth experiment rather than predict its result."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:1a6a0f20c79d",
  "problem": "How to interpret signs of scheming or misalignment in model behaviour or reasoning, given ambiguity about whether they reflect noise.",
  "did": "Beth warns against treating ambiguous misalignment evidence as noise and patching it superficially, and argues against training models to suppress visible scheming in the chain of thought.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "training the model not to do that and slapping patches on it",
   "penalising scheming seen in the chain of thought"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Superficial fixes make the evidence ambiguous enough that behaviour won't change, and penalising visible scheming may just teach the model to hide it."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:345ccc39500a",
  "problem": "Value leakage might be limited to one kind of value.",
  "did": "Tested several types of values: moral preferences, loyalty to the developer company, and preferences among human leisure activities. They also compared multiple frontier models, including Claude and Qwen.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Not stated in the abstract. The implied aim is to show the phenomenon is general."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:4b5cf8921966",
  "problem": "How to prevent detectors from exploiting dataset artifacts such as explicit lie instructions in system prompts.",
  "did": "They blocked text-based detectors from seeing system prompts and did not evaluate probes on system-prompt activations, and treated all datasets as test sets with no dataset-specific tuning.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "giving detectors full access to system prompts"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The lie instructions are unrealistic artifacts of the dataset that would let text-based detectors reliably detect lies."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:5ee2f7d5e7dd",
  "problem": "How to treat uncertainty about the hacking capabilities of internally deployed misaligned agents.",
  "did": "Stated an assumption that misaligned agents can hack internal and external systems, likely beyond public evidence, unless shown otherwise.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "assuming capabilities match only what is publicly observed"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Agents have shown demonstrably superhuman hacking capability and patching efforts remain incomplete, as the Hugging Face incident showed."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:981023656452",
  "problem": "How to scope a paper's experiments and claims so it is neither unfocused nor missing obvious extensions.",
  "did": "Keep every experiment tied to one core idea while still ensuring the paper has no obvious unaddressed improvements, leaving only minor open directions.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "running every possible experiment related to the idea",
   "leaving obvious questions unanswered"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Running everything distracts readers from the key idea, but missing obvious improvements leaves readers unsatisfied."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:388cdd3829c8",
  "problem": "How to elicit forecasts so that calibration of respondents can be assessed before the outcomes are known.",
  "did": "Asked for 90% confidence intervals rather than point estimates or simple yes/no predictions, enabling analysis of overconfidence from the answer distributions alone.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "asking \"how many math theorems will an AI solve?\" as a point estimate"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Interval answers let the author analyze calibration now, since it is too early to grade correctness."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:58bf13fed636",
  "problem": "How strongly to state the main contribution and limits of the findings",
  "did": "Framed the empirical result as the main contribution and listed limitations (small models, LoRA, constructed poison, lenient judge)",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "claim a mechanistic explanation"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The regression model is only illustrative, so the empirical result is what the authors stand behind."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:341a73d5e2c0",
  "problem": "How to design the participation process so that frontier companies would take part in the pilot assessment.",
  "did": "They offered a silent/no-fault exit option allowing participants to withdraw, shaping the process around maintaining relationships with companies.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "a process without an exit option"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "METR's work relies on developing and maintaining strong working relationships with companies."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:b6dfae13dc8f",
  "problem": "Whether METR should prioritize developing evaluation science or becoming an auditor of frontier models.",
  "did": "METR made developing the science of evaluations its top priority and treated becoming an auditor as unnecessary for that goal.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "becoming an auditor"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "METR does not need to be an auditor in order to succeed at developing the science of evaluations."
 }
]
